known_relations: B f rises from 0.01381 at 0 h to 0.08918 at 24 h; A is about 0.0044 at 8-24 h. Fields and objects are not independent preparation replicates (initial_measurements.json).

hypotheses.statement: At fixed reaction chemistry, increasing measured variant/reference RNA loading changes relative phase selectivity, potentially shifting from variant enrichment in the dense phase toward weaker or reversed partitioning. If the resulting variant-enriched dilute domains form or persist inside a reference-rich dense network, they can appear as internal cavities. C2L1-alpha shows different endpoint selectivity ranges, but does not establish the loading dependence or the phase-domain-to-cavity bridge.

The phase endpoints are not comparable to the imaging reaction or do not represent its mixture range; cavities arise from amplification carryover or another reaction-state change independently of composition-driven internal domains. A constant selectivity across matched loading conditions remains possible until a controlled series is measured.

gaps.description: Determine whether relative partition selectivity changes with measured mixture composition under matched conditions, and whether that predicts internal cavities. Current endpoint differences do not identify a composition response or causal link.
No mapping from bulk phase concentrations/volumes to image f, and no causal separation from carryover or population/measurement alternatives.

reply.summary: Target: explain the emergence and persistence of the image-derived per-droplet arithmetic mean empty-area fraction f(t), not infer RNA concentration from DNA read fractions. At 0–24 h, A falls from 0.01487 to about 0.0044 while B rises from 0.01381 to 0.08918; fields/objects are not independent preparation replicates. C01 reports a 94.66% reference DNA read fraction and heterogeneous longer/shorter reads, but DNA frequencies do not determine transcribed RNA abundance. E02 shows single-preparation endpoint differences among gel-purified length fractions (M near zero, M+L 0.0445, M+S 0.0941), without matched carryover controls or RNA yield. C04 supplies phase concentration endpoints: point estimates give variant/reference partition selectivity alpha=(Cv,dense/Cv,dilute)/(Cr,dense/Cr,dilute) of about 37.9 at tie-line 1 and 0.335 at tie-line 2; zero variant concentrations make tie-line 0 undefined, and conservative intervals overlap unity at tie-line 2. These endpoints motivate but do not establish composition-dependent selectivity or its connection to image cavities. C03 confirms the available tracking lacks longitudinal same-droplet cavity state/area and track-ending reasons. Main task: compute selectivity and its uncertainty correctly, compare with the meaningful constant-selectivity alternative, and state a discriminating prediction without equating area fraction to concentration or phase volume.

hypotheses.statement: At fixed reaction chemistry, increasing the variant-to-reference RNA loading changes relative phase selectivity non-monotonically: variant enrichment in the dense phase at lower loading gives way to weaker variant partitioning at higher loading. If this creates or stabilizes variant-enriched dilute domains inside a reference-rich dense network, their area can appear as internal cavities. This phase-selectivity-to-cavity bridge is not established by the supplied endpoints.

Relative phase selectivity is constant (or the observed endpoints do not represent the B reaction); cavities arise from another amplification-associated factor such as reaction carryover or an unmeasured reaction-state change, independently of composition-driven internal domain formation.

request.purpose: Quantify relative partition selectivity from observed endpoints and check whether the changing-selectivity hypothesis is distinguishable from alpha=1 or constant selectivity within supplied conservative error ranges.
request.model_spec: For each tie_line_id, use dilute and dense records in DATA['phase_measurements.json']; concentrations in ng/uL. Compute K_ref=Cr_dense/Cr_dilute and K_variant=Cv_dense/Cv_dilute when denominators are positive, then alpha=K_variant/K_ref. Propagate provided asymmetric errors as rectangular worst-case bounds: K_lo=(Cd-dense_lower)/(Cl+dilute_upper), K_hi=(Cd+dense_upper)/(Cl-dilute_lower), and alpha bounds as K_variant_lo/K_ref_hi and K_variant_hi/K_ref_lo when positive. Report exact status if any denominator is zero/nonpositive. Compare alpha point estimates and intervals across tie-line indices, explicitly stating that index is not established as composition. Null comparator: constant alpha=1 (nonselective relative partitioning); do not fit a composition response curve from three endpoints. Output the assay-matched conditional prediction and limitations separately from arithmetic results.

sources.title: Differential interactions determine anisotropies at interfaces of RNA-based biomolecular condensates.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Biomolecular condensates form via macromolecular phase separation. Here, we report results from our characterization of synthetic condensates formed by phase separation of mixtures comprising two types of RNA molecules and the biocompatible polymer polyethylene glycol. Purine-rich RNAs are scaffolds that drive phase separation via heterotypic interactions. Conversely, pyrimidine-rich RNA molecules are adsorbents defined by weaker heterotypic interactions. They adsorb onto and wet the interfaces of coexisting phases formed by scaffolds. Lattice-based simulations reproduce the phenomenology observed in experiments and these simulations predict that scaffolds and adsorbents have different non-random orientational preferences at interfaces. Dynamics at interfaces were probed using single-molecule tracking of fluorogenic probes bound to RNA molecules. These experiments revealed dynamical anisotropy at interfaces whereby motions of probe molecules parallel to the interface are faster than motions perpendicular to the interface. Taken together, our findings have broad implications for designing synthetic condensates with tunable interfacial properties.

sources.title: Converging frontiers in biomolecular condensate and synthetic cell research.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Biomolecular condensate and artificial cell research, though distinct in origin, share a focus on studying and mimicking (sub)cellular compartments. Identifying converging frontiers offers opportunities to advance both fields. Possibilities arise in areas where the condensate structure-function relationship is most prevalent. This includes interfaces, active systems, multiphases, aging, and applying in silico tools. This perspective aims to provide insight in how recent developments can drive convergence of the fields.

sources.title: Emerging roles of transcriptional condensates as temporal signal integrators.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Transcription factors relay information from the external environment to gene regulatory networks that control cell physiology. To confer signalling specificity, robustness and coordination, these signalling networks use temporal communication codes, such as the amplitude, duration or frequency of signals. Although much is known about how temporal information is encoded, a mechanistic understanding of how gene regulatory networks decode signalling dynamics is lacking. Recent advances in our understanding of phase separation of transcriptional condensates provide new biophysical frameworks for both temporal encoding and decoding mechanisms. In this Perspective, we summarize the mechanisms by which transcriptional condensates could enable temporal decoding through signal adaptation, memory and persistence. We further outline methods to probe and manipulate dynamic communication codes of transcription factors and condensates to rationally control gene activation.

sources.title: Engineering Protein-Polyelectrolyte Interactions for Cellular Applications.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Protein-polyelectrolyte interactions are fundamental interactions in biology that occur at every length scale, from protein-DNA complexes to phase-separated organelles. They drive processes ranging from gene transcription and DNA synthesis to viral assembly. Protein engineering is a powerful way to modulate these interactions, both to probe endogenous function and to engineer novel interactions between species. In this review, we consider the various noncovalent interactions that govern the formation and behavior of these complexes, and we discuss how protein modifications such as changes to structure, charge, and charge patterning affect them. We highlight recent examples where engineering changes to protein-polyelectrolyte interactions have helped elucidate biological function, and we then focus on recent efforts toward de novo material design of synthetic biomolecular condensates and functional nanoassemblies.

sources.title: Pathological mutation in SMN impairs modulation of GAR1 phase separation linking condensate dysfunction to Spinal Muscular Atrophy
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Summary   Pathological mutations in liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) scaffold proteins have been linked to biomolecular condensate dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases, while the possible impact of client protein mutations remains unclear. In spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), the disease-associated E134K mutation in the Tudor domain (TD) of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein disrupts its interaction with GAR1, an RGG-rich protein within the H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex. The consequences of this impaired interaction have not been elucidated. Here, we identified GAR1 as an LLPS scaffold protein that is phase separated in nuclear compartments and forms gel-like condensates via complex coacervation with RNA  in vitro . In cells, we reveal that SMN co-localizes with GAR1 in Cajal bodies and modulates its dynamics. Using confocal microscopy and NMR spectroscopy, we further show that SMN TD is a client protein that regulates the architecture and dynamics of GAR1 condensates through competitive RNA interactions, implicating GAR1 phase separation in RNA accumulation and release processes regulated by SMN. Notably, the SMA-associated E134K variant of SMN exhibits a reduced affinity for GAR1, impairing the modulation of GAR1 condensates and displacement RNA. Our findings suggest a mechanistic link between phase separation dysregulation and SMA, driven by disrupted scaffold-client interactions, that highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting SMN-dependent condensate regulation in SMA.
